ceb.title: Papasya - Masunod ni Pedro
ceb.question: Giunsa gikan ni Pedro ang modernong Papa?
ceb.answer: Sumala sa doktrina sa Katolisismo, ang Papa mao'y masunod ni Pedro isip Obispo sa Roma. Ni Kristo gihatag kang Pedro ang usa ka espesyal nga katungdanan sa pagpangulo sa simbahan (Mateo 16:18-19). Kining katungdanan gipasar sa mga obispo sa Roma pinaagi sa apostolikong pagmasunod. Ang Papa nagsilbi isip visible head sa simbahan unibersal, nga nagpahigayon sa pag-espirituhanon nga pag-ulo ni Pedro sa tibuuk kalibutan.

en.title: Apostolic Succession and the Papacy
en.question: How can a bishop today claim the authority Jesus gave to Peter two thousand years ago?
en.answer: Apostolic succession is the unbroken transmission of the office and authority Christ gave the Apostles, handed on through the laying on of hands from generation to generation. The Apostles clearly intended their office to continue: when Judas fell, the Eleven chose Matthias to take his 'office' (Acts 1:20-26, quoting Ps 109:8), showing that apostolic ministry is an office that passes to a successor, not a personal privilege that dies with the man. Paul instructs Timothy to entrust what he received to reliable men who will teach others in turn (2 Tim 2:2), a fourfold chain of succession. Just as Peter held a unique primacy among the Apostles, that primacy passes to his successor, the Bishop of Rome, where Peter established his see and was martyred. The early Fathers listed the Roman bishops in unbroken order precisely to prove the authenticity of their teaching against innovators. This visible, historical continuity guarantees that the Church today teaches with the very authority Christ conferred.
en.answer_full:
> "The blessed Peter, the head and prince of the apostles, the pillar of faith and the foundation of the Catholic Church, received the keys of the kingdom from our Lord Jesus Christ." — Pope Leo the Great, *Sermon 3*

The question of how a bishop today can claim the authority Jesus gave to Peter is one of the most important questions in Christian theology. It touches the nature of the Church itself: is the Church a community that looks back only to a written deposit, or is it a living institution in which Christ's authority is actively exercised by appointed shepherds? The Catholic answer is the latter, grounded in the doctrine of **apostolic succession** — the unbroken chain of ordained bishops stretching from the present moment back to the apostles themselves.

Two claims require defense. First, that Christ gave Peter a unique, transferable authority. Second, that this authority has been faithfully transmitted to the Bishop of Rome. Both claims are supported by Scripture, by the testimony of the earliest Christians, and by the logic of how divine institutions operate in history.

---

## The Biblical Foundation of Peter's Authority

### Matthew 16:18–19 — The Foundational Text

The most direct evidence is found in Matthew 16:18–19. When Simon confesses that Jesus is "the Christ, the Son of the living God," Jesus responds with a triple declaration: he gives Simon the new name *Petros* (Rock), promises to build his *ekklesia* on this rock, and grants him "the keys of the kingdom of heaven" with the power to bind and loose.

Each element demands attention. The name-change is covenantal — in Scripture, God changes names when he establishes a new role: Abram becomes Abraham, Jacob becomes Israel. Jesus changing Simon's name to "Rock" at this precise moment signals an office, not merely a compliment. The **keys of the kingdom** are drawn from Isaiah 22:22, where the prophet describes Eliakim receiving "the key of the house of David" — becoming the royal steward who holds authority in the king's name. Crucially, this is an *office* that passes from person to person; the key is handed on. The power to **bind and loose** (from the Aramaic *asar* and *shera*) is rabbinical language for authoritative doctrinal and disciplinary decisions — decisions whose validity is ratified in heaven.

### Luke 22:31–32 — The Commission to Strengthen

On the night of the Last Supper, Jesus tells Simon Peter: "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you all [the Greek *hymas* is plural], that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you [*sou*, singular] that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, *strengthen your brothers*." Christ singles Peter out for special intercessory prayer and assigns him a unique post-resurrection pastoral role over the other apostles. This is not general encouragement; it is a designated office of confirmation.

### John 21:15–17 — The Triple Commissioning

After the Resurrection, Jesus asks Peter three times "Do you love me?" and three times charges him: "Feed my lambs… tend my sheep… feed my sheep." The triple repetition corresponds to Peter's threefold denial and serves as a formal reinstatement and commissioning. The word for shepherd (*poimainein*) is the same word used of Christ himself in John 10. Peter is appointed under-shepherd over the entirety of Christ's flock — not over one community but over the whole.

---

## The Nature of the Petrine Office

### Office versus Person

The foundational theological distinction is between the **person** and the **office**. Catholic doctrine does not claim that Peter's personal sanctity or individual genius was transmitted to Rome. It claims that Christ established a *permanent ministry* — a structural role in the life of the Church — which was intended to outlive Peter just as the Davidic office outlived David.

This is consistent with the logic of every divine institution in Scripture. The Aaronic priesthood was not abolished when Aaron died; the Davidic throne did not cease when David died. Jesus, who came not to abolish but to fulfill, established an office with the intention that it continue. When Peter died, the question for the early Church was not "does this office still exist?" but "who now holds it?"

### Why Rome?

The association with Rome flows from Peter's own presence, ministry, and martyrdom there. It is attested by Clement, Ignatius, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Eusebius, among others. The logic is that of the royal capital: the authority of the steward who holds the key of David is exercised from the seat of governance. Rome was where Peter exercised his final and supreme pastoral authority and where he sealed it with his blood.

---

## Apostolic Succession: The Mechanism of Continuity

**Apostolic succession** operates through the laying on of hands in episcopal ordination. Each bishop receives the fullness of holy orders — including the authority to teach, sanctify, and govern — through an unbroken chain of ordinations reaching back to the apostles. This is not a legal fiction; it is the sacramental reality the Church has always understood itself to possess.

Irenaeus of Lyon (c. AD 180) articulates the principle with precision:

> "It is possible for everyone in every church, who wishes to see the truth, to contemplate clearly the tradition of the apostles manifested throughout the whole world; and we are in a position to reckon up those who were by the apostles instituted bishops in the churches, and the succession of these men to our own times." — *Against Heresies* III.3.1

The list matters because deviation from the apostolic deposit would be detectable at the point of rupture. Succession is the chain of custody for apostolic faith.

---

## Patristic Testimony

### Clement of Rome (c. AD 96)

Writing to the Corinthians, Clement intervenes to rebuke them for deposing their presbyters — not because the Corinthians asked Roman opinion, but because Rome considered it its responsibility:

> "But if any disobey the words spoken by Him through us, let them know that they will involve themselves in transgression and in no small danger." — *1 Clement* 59

This unsolicited exercise of authority over a distant community is inexplicable unless Rome was understood to possess trans-local jurisdiction from the earliest years.

### Ignatius of Antioch (c. AD 107)

In his letter to the Romans, Ignatius describes the Roman church in terms that carry more than honorary weight when read against his other letters, where he uses similar language to describe the authority of local bishops:

> "You have never envied anyone; you have taught others. Now I desire that those things may be confirmed which you enjoin in your instructions. Only pray to God for me, that, by these instruments, I may be found a sacrifice to God." — *Letter to the Romans*, Prologue

### Irenaeus of Lyon (c. AD 180)

Irenaeus provides the most explicit early statement of Roman primacy:

> "It is a matter of necessity that every Church should agree with this Church, on account of its preeminent authority (*propter potentiorem principalitatem*)." — *Against Heresies* III.3.2

---

## Conciliar and Magisterial Definition

The First Vatican Council (1870) defined in *Pastor Aeternus* that when the Roman Pontiff speaks *ex cathedra* on matters of faith and morals, he is protected from error by the divine assistance promised to Peter. The Second Vatican Council (*Lumen Gentium* 22) complemented this by affirming the college of bishops in union with the Pope as co-possessors of supreme teaching authority — ensuring primacy is never exercised in isolation from the episcopal college.

| Reference | Teaching |
|---|---|
| CCC 77 | Apostolic Tradition is transmitted through the apostolic succession of bishops |
| CCC 861 | Bishops are successors of the apostles through the Holy Spirit |
| CCC 862 | The college of bishops succeeds the college of apostles |
| CCC 882 | The Pope has full, supreme, and universal power over the whole Church |
| CCC 891 | The charism of infallibility extends to the whole Church and is exercised by the Pope |

---

## Common Objections

**"Paul rebuked Peter, so Peter had no supreme authority."** Paul's correction of Peter in Galatians 2 is a correction of *behavior*, not of office. Popes can act inconsistently with the faith they are commissioned to protect; papal infallibility covers formal definitions, not personal conduct. The rebuke confirms accountability, not the absence of authority.

**"The word 'rock' in Matthew 16 refers to Peter's confession, not to Peter himself."** The Aramaic spoken by Jesus uses *Kepha* for both the name and the rock — there is no linguistic gap. The most natural reading, affirmed by Origen, Chrysostom, and the majority of Fathers, is that Peter himself is the rock on which the Church is built.

**"Bishops are not mentioned as successors of apostles in Scripture."** The principle is clear even if the technical vocabulary develops later: Acts 1 shows the apostles replacing Judas by communal appointment, establishing that apostolic roles are transferable offices. The Pastoral Epistles describe the bishop as the governing officer of the local church — a role received by appointment and transmitted to others (2 Timothy 2:2).

---

## Conclusion

The claim that a bishop today holds Petrine authority is the conclusion of careful exegesis, the testimony of the earliest Christian writers, and the structural logic of the institution Christ founded. The keys given to Peter were designed to be carried forward — generation after generation, bishop after bishop — until the Shepherd himself returns. The line from Peter to Rome to the present is the line along which the living authority of Christ runs through history.

tl.title: Paghalili ng Papa kay San Pedro
tl.question: Paano ang Simbahang Katoliko ay nagsasabing ang mga papa ay mga kahalili ni San Pedro?
tl.answer: Ang Simbahang Katoliko ay nakabatay ang paghalili ng papa sa mga salita ni Cristo kay Pedro sa Mateo 16:18-19, kung saan Ibinigay Niya kay Pedro ang mga susi sa kaharian at ang awtoridad na magbiroo at magpabuklod. Si Pedro ay malinaw na pinuno ng mga apostol, at ang kasaysayang ebidensya ay nagpapakita ng hindi napuputol na linya ng mga obispo ng Roma na bumabalik kay Pedro. Ang paghaliling ito ay pinananatili sa pamamagitan ng paglalagay ng mga kamay sa apostolikong paghalili.
